newsitem.title: INDIA: India's BHEL net races past forecasts.
newsitem.headline: India's BHEL net races past forecasts.

text.p: Robust sales to India's power sector drove the 1996/97 (April-March) net profit of equipment maker Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd (BHEL) sharply above market expectations, analysts said on Thursday.
State-run BHEL -- among the country's top 25 firms -- said its net profit surged nearly 34 percent to 4.68 billion rupees ($130 million), from 3.5 billion in 1995/96.
Analysts said the results beat all market expectations with the average consensus net profit forecast pegged as low as 3.8 billion rupees.
BHEL shares vaulted 21.75 rupees, or 6.6 percent, to close at 351.75 rupees on the Bombay Stock Exchange after the earnings announcement.
The company said its turnover during 1996/97 jumped to 57.40 billion rupees from 48.33 billion a year earlier.
An analyst at a leading U.S. brokerage said higher than anticipated sales during February and March had contributed substantially to profits.
"We estimated a turnover of 52.5 billion rupees but in the last one-and-a-half months of the year they did an additional five billion rupees," he said.
"At the net level, this has meant another 800 to 900 billion added to profit," the analyst added.
"Large orders from the power sector made up for a slowdown in the company's industry division," he said, adding that he had a strong buy recommendation on the company's stock.
BHEL said order inflows in the power sector hit a record level of 40.48 billion rupees -- two-and-a-half times that of last year's achievement.

"These included orders for 2,556 MW of power plant equipment," the firm said in a statement. "The performance has been achieved while operating in a highly competitive environment and the general slowdown trend in industry."
Industrial growth as measured by the index of industrial production grew by 9.1 percent during April-November 1996 against 11.7 percent a year earlier, latest data show.
Analysts said low material costs which include costs of raw materials and payment to sub-contracters had resulted in improved margins.
"Their material cost has gone up only by 6.4 percent while sales are up by 18.8 percent," said an analyst at securities firm James Capel B&K.
"Margins have thus improved to 18.3 percent from 15.4 percent," he said.
"A substantial chunk of the rise in profits seems to have come because the company has saved on the raw materials front," agreed an analyst at Jardine Fleming India Broking.
